paras: The lynching of John Adams was the hanging of a man described as 'a half-breed Mexican' by about thirty of his neighbors near Pit River in Big Valley, Lassen County, California, on the night of February 24, 1882. Accused of horse stealing, Adams had defied a committee that ordered him to leave, and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union reported the killing as the work of 'the Vigilantes'.

According to C. A. McCash of Adir, Modoc County, who brought the news to the Record-Union, Adams had been in that part of the country for some time, accused of stealing horses, committing 'other depredations' and terrorizing the people. The paper noted that the section was sparsely settled and that 'the law's protection is a weak arm indeed.' The neighbors met and sent a committee to tell Adams to leave, but he reportedly laughed at them, said there were not enough men in the state to hang him, and boasted of his thefts.

When the time he had been given ran out, the neighbors met again on Friday night and agreed that he should be lynched. Some thirty men went at about 11 o'clock to a house near the banks of Pit River where Adams was staying and hid to watch for him. As he crossed to the barn they seized and bound him, carried him to an oak tree, and hanged him.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and no one in the mob was named.

The Record-Union printed the only full account on March 1 under the headline 'They Meant Business', calling Adams 'an old criminal and desperado' and taking the vigilantes' charges against him as fact. A shorter version from the Reno Journal, which repeated the Record-Union's wording and dated the hanging to 'the night of the 24th ultimo,' ran in the Gold Hill Daily News on March 3 under 'Judge Lynch'. The Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, reprinted the same paragraph without comment on March 4. None of these papers described Adams as Black.

bases: About thirty neighbors, called 'the Vigilantes', seized John Adams at night and hanged him from an oak tree after accusing him of horse stealing (A2, A3).

A2 reports that some thirty neighbors, acting without any officer and after a 'verdict of all' that he should be lynched, seized and hanged Adams for alleged horse stealing and other depredations; A3 calls it lynching 'by the people of Big Valley'.
The only full account is the Sacramento Record-Union's interview with C. A. McCash (A2); the Reno Journal paragraph carried by A3 and A4 repeats A2's wording and is not an independent report.

accounts.label: Reno Journal paragraph
accounts.gist: Adams was lynched by the people of Big Valley on the night of the 24th after laughing at the committee and boasting he was an outlaw.

framing.detail: Under 'They Meant Business' the Record-Union calls Adams 'an old criminal and desperado' and explains the hanging by the weakness of the law in a sparsely settled section.
Nevada papers ran the Reno Journal's short paragraph under 'Judge Lynch' or among state news items without comment.
